section.title: Warning examples
section.p: Continuity gave us two promises. The Intermediate Value Theorem says that a continuous graph cannot skip a height. The Extreme Value Theorem says that a continuous function on a closed finite interval reaches a highest and lowest value.
Those promises are strong because their hypotheses are strong. If we remove a hypothesis, the conclusion may fail.
This section gathers the warnings in one place. Each example is small, but each one protects a theorem from being used illegally.

subsection.title: A function with no limit at a jump
subsection.p: A two-sided limit needs one target. A jump gives two targets.
Define
As x\to 0^-, the values of J(x) are always 0. So
As x\to 0^+, the values of J(x) are always 1. So
The one-sided limits disagree. Therefore
does not exist.

figure.caption: A jump creates two different one-sided limits, so the two-sided limit fails.

subsection.p: Changing the value at x=0 cannot repair the two-sided limit. The problem is not the point itself. The problem is that the nearby values on the two sides head toward different numbers.
A two-sided limit is about agreement from both sides.

subsection.title: A limit that is infinite, not finite
subsection.p: A different kind of failure happens when the values do not settle near any finite number.
Consider
As x gets close to 0, the denominator x^2 gets close to 0, but stays positive. The quotient grows larger and larger.
We write
This notation does not mean that the function has a finite limit. It means the values grow beyond every fixed positive bound.
There is no real number L such that \lim_{x\to 0}\frac{1}{x^2}=L.

figure.caption: The values of 1/x^2 grow without bound near 0. This is infinite behavior, not a finite limit.

subsection.p: A removable discontinuity can be repaired by filling in one value. Infinite divergent behavior cannot. No choice of f(0) can keep the nearby values close to a finite number.
\infty describes unbounded behavior. It is not a real-number target.

subsection.title: The Intermediate Value Theorem fails without continuity
subsection.p: The Intermediate Value Theorem said:
subsection.md: \text{continuous graph}+\text{endpoint values} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{all intermediate values are hit.}
subsection.p: The word continuous cannot be removed.
Define
On the interval [-1,1], S(-1)=0 and S(1)=2.
The number 1 lies between 0 and 2. If we tried to use the Intermediate Value Theorem, we might expect some c\in [-1,1] such that S(c)=1.
But no such c exists. The function takes only the values 0 and 2. It jumps over 1.

figure.caption: Without continuity, a function can jump over an intermediate value.

subsection.p: The theorem fails because S is not continuous at 0.
The Intermediate Value Theorem is a no-jump theorem.

subsection.title: The Extreme Value Theorem fails on an open interval
subsection.p: The Extreme Value Theorem said:
subsection.md: \text{continuous on }[a,b] \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{absolute maximum and minimum are reached.}
subsection.p: The closed interval [a,b] includes its endpoints. If the endpoints are missing, the conclusion can fail.
Consider
on the open interval (0,1).
The function is continuous at every point of its domain. Its values get close to 1, but never equal 1, because x=1 is not in the interval.
So f has no absolute maximum on (0,1).
The values also get close to 0, but never equal 0, because x=0 is not in the interval.
So f has no absolute minimum on (0,1).

figure.caption: On (0,1), the function f(x)=x approaches its lowest and highest possible values but never reaches them.

subsection.p: The problem is not the formula. The formula f(x)=x is perfectly continuous. The problem is the domain. The endpoints are missing.
For the Extreme Value Theorem, endpoints matter.

subsection.title: The Extreme Value Theorem fails on an unbounded interval
subsection.p: A closed interval is not enough if it stretches forever.
Consider f(x)=x on [0,\infty).
The function is continuous on its domain. The interval includes its left endpoint 0, so f has an absolute minimum:
But f has no absolute maximum. Given any value f(x)=x, we can choose a larger input, such as x+1, and get
So no largest value exists.
A physical version is also common. Recall the cooling model
The interval [0,\infty) is unbounded. The temperature starts at T(0)=160, and approaches 70 as t\to\infty. It never reaches 70 for any finite t, because \frac{90}{t+1}\gt 0.
So this continuous function has an absolute maximum on [0,\infty), but no absolute minimum.
A function can approach a best value forever without reaching it.
The word bounded in the Extreme Value Theorem prevents this escape to infinity.

subsection.title: A map of the warnings
subsection.p: The examples above are not exceptions to the theorems. They are reminders of what the theorems actually say.

subsection.p: A theorem is a machine with conditions. If a condition is missing, the output is no longer guaranteed.
Limits and continuity have now given us a careful language for functions of a real variable x. But some limiting processes arrive as lists:
